423	## 7. Execution design
424	
425	### 7.1 Binding the target to a column
426	
427	`model.MeasureAgg` gains `TagName`, `TagFamily` and `HideTag` (the last set when the analyzer
428	injected the projection). Four existing seams become target-aware:
429	
430	| Seam | Change |
431	|---|---|
432	| `plan/analyzer.go:209 translateAgg` | resolve tag **or** field; enforce the §6 matrix |
433	| `plan/analyzer.go:264 ensureAggFieldProjected` | mirror `ensureGroupByProjected` (`:226`) and inject the tag, setting `HideTag` |
434	| `integration.go:139 buildNativeTagSet` | include the agg tag, so its column is native typed |
435	| `plan.go:155 lookupFieldColumnIndex` | add a tag sibling resolving on `(RoleTag, TagFamily, Name)`, like `lookupGroupByKeyIndices` (`:135`) |
436	
437	The `buildNativeTagSet` change is load-bearing: without it the target column is a
438	`ColumnTypeTagValue` passthrough and `fold` panics on its type assertion. This is the same
439	native-column contract the analyzer already documents at `analyzer.go:73-79`.
440	
441	Everything downstream of `AggSpec.InputCol` is index-based, so **SUM/MIN/MAX/MEAN/COUNT over an
442	INT tag need no execution changes at all** — the partial is a `RoleField` int64/float64 column
443	named after the target, exactly what `bindAggReduceSpecs` (`reduce.go:219`) already binds. Only
444	two small operator fixes are needed:
445	
446	- `aggregation.go:464 fold` — `COUNT` must not read the value for non-numeric columns (it
447	  currently parses, then calls `In(v)`). A null-check-only branch makes `COUNT(string_tag)` work.
448	- `aggregation.go:252 collectTagIndices` — accept an exclusion index so a `HideTag` target is
449	  not emitted as a first-seen tag beside its own result field.
450	
451	### 7.2 Time-bucket grouping
452	
453	The implementation is one small map operator plus one conditional in the output layout. The key
454	insight is that **the timestamp is already an `int64` column** in the input schema
455	(`RoleTimestamp`, produced by `BuildBatchSchema`'s fixed prefix at `integration.go:64-69`), and
456	`appendKeyComponent` already encodes `int64` key components. So the bucket does not need a new
457	key encoder, a derived column, or a change to `computeKey`:
458	
459	> **Floor the timestamp column in place, then group by it like any other column.**
460	
461	A `BatchTimeBucket` map operator sits immediately before the aggregation and rewrites the
462	timestamp column to its bucket start:
463	
464	```go
465	// bucketStart mirrors pkg/flow/streaming/sliding_window.go:302 getWindowStart,
466	// the formula the TopN pre-aggregation path already uses to assign tumbling
467	// windows. It is exactly DATE_BIN with a Unix-epoch origin.
468	func bucketStart(ts, width int64) int64 { return ts - ts%width }
469	```
470	
471	#### The bucket group must NOT be a hash map over all buckets
472	
473	The obvious implementation — add the bucket to `keyIndices` and let `BatchAggregation`'s
474	`map[string]*aggGroup` hold every `(bucket, tags…)` combination until the scan ends — is the
475	wrong shape for a time-series database. It holds `buckets × tagGroups` live groups, blocks until
476	the last row is read, and then needs a sort to put the series back in time order. All three costs
477	are avoidable, because **the input is already sorted by time**.
478	
479	`applyMeasureQueryOrdering` (`banyand/measure/query.go:286`) sets the default explicitly:
480	
481	```go
482	func applyMeasureQueryOrdering(mqo model.MeasureQueryOptions, result *queryResult) {
483		if mqo.Order == nil {
484			result.ascTS = true
485			result.orderByTS = true      // ← globally timestamp-ascending
486			return
487		}
488		…
489		result.orderByTS = mqo.Order.Type == index.OrderByTypeTime
490	}
491	```
492	
493	and `queryResult.Less` (`:913`) then makes the merge heap compare **timestamp first**, falling
494	back to seriesID only to break ties. An aggregation request carries no `order_by` — the
495	distributed analyzer explicitly skips OrderBy resolution when `Agg != nil`
496	(`distributed.go:248`) — so `Order == nil`, and rows arrive in globally ascending timestamp
497	order with no change to the scan at all. (The non-default branch, `orderByTS == false`, sorts by
498	`sidToIndex` first and is series-major; that is the case the guard below exists for.)
499	
500	Sorted input means a bucket, once left behind, can never receive another row. So:
501	
502	> **Stream the buckets.** Keep groups for the *current* bucket only; when a row's bucket advances,
503	> flush that bucket's groups downstream and reset the map.
504	
505	```
506	rows (time-ascending) ──▶ [bucket B0 groups] flush ──▶ [B1 groups] flush ──▶ [B2 …]
507	                           ^ map holds ONE bucket at a time
508	```
509	
510	Three properties fall out, and they are the reason to prefer this over the map:
511	
512	| | Hash map over all buckets | Streaming |
513	|---|---|---|
514	| Live groups | `buckets × tagGroups` | `tagGroups` (one bucket) |
515	| Emission | blocking — nothing until the scan ends | node-local pipelining — bucket *n* leaves the operator while *n+1* fills |
516	| Output order | needs a sort pass | already bucket-ascending |
517	
518	The 1440× memory multiplier a 24-hour/1-minute query would otherwise carry simply does not exist,
519	and `BatchAggregation`'s `BreakerOperator` contract (`vectorized/operator.go:63` — "buffers all
520	input via Consume, then produces output via NextBatch") relaxes to a pipelined operator for the
521	bucketed case. This also mirrors how the codebase already aggregates over time on the write path:
522	`pkg/flow/streaming` assigns tumbling windows and emits them as they close, using the same
523	`getWindowStart` formula.
524	
525	**"Relaxes to a pipelined operator" is not a small tweak to `BreakerOperator` — it needed a new
526	operator shape.** `BreakerOperator` is driven by `breakerStage`, which fully drains upstream via
527	repeated `Consume` calls before it ever calls the breaker's own `NextBatch` — by contract, not by
528	a fixable oversight. Wrapping `BatchTimeBucket` as a `BreakerOperator` would therefore have pulled
529	every upstream batch, closing every bucket the whole scan will ever produce, before emitting the
530	first one: exactly the `buckets × tagGroups` cost this section exists to avoid, just moved from
531	the group map into an output queue. (This is precisely the failure mode §11's testing strategy
532	calls out under "Pipelining": *"A `BreakerOperator`-shaped implementation passes every correctness
533	test and fails this one."*)
534	
535	The actual fix: `BatchTimeBucket` is a genuine `vectorized.PullOperator` that owns and pulls from
536	its upstream directly inside its own `NextBatch`, rather than being driven by `breakerStage`. It
537	is spliced into the pipeline via a new `PipelineBuilder.Transform(fn func(upstream PullOperator)
538	PullOperator)` method (`pkg/query/vectorized/pipeline.go`) — it closes whatever has been built so
539	far into one concrete `PullOperator`, hands it to `fn`, and makes `fn`'s result the new base for
540	whatever follows. `Transform` is now general pipeline infrastructure, available to any future
541	operator with the same requirement: pull upstream lazily, batch by batch, rather than draining it
542	before serving anything. (COUNT_DISTINCT, §7.3–§7.4, does not need it — it reuses
543	`BatchAggregation`'s existing `Consume`/`NextBatch` contract unchanged.)
544	
545	A related pitfall surfaced during review even after the `PullOperator` rewrite: `BatchTimeBucket`
546	originally still drained a closed bucket's aggregator in one synchronous loop before returning
547	anything. That is harmless for the streaming path (one bucket's groups are bounded by construction
548	either way), but index mode's non-streaming aggregator can represent the *entire* scan — so
549	draining it in one shot re-introduced the same "materialize everything before returning the first
550	batch" shape this whole design exists to avoid, just at the output-queue layer instead of the
551	group-map layer. The fix (`drainMapModeAggregator`) pulls that terminal aggregator one page at a
552	time, interleaved with normal output commits, the same discipline the upstream pull loop already
553	follows. Any future operator that holds one aggregator across an entire unordered scan — a
554	candidate shape for other index-mode fallbacks — should drain it the same way.
555	
556	**Index mode does not get this guarantee, and must not stream.** `query.go:140-147` returns
557	through the index-mode branch *before* the ordering setup above ever runs; `buildIndexQueryResult`
558	passes `mqo.Order` through unchanged (`query.go:506-560`), and with a nil order
559	`storage/index.go:350-374` takes the unsorted filter path and returns the underlying index search
560	order. Timestamps being present in `SeriesData` is not an ordering guarantee. A legal index-mode
561	input can therefore arrive in buckets B, A, B — which would reopen a flushed bucket, or trip the
562	monotonicity guard on a query that is perfectly valid.
563	
564	> **Index-mode bucketed aggregation uses the non-streaming map** — groups keyed on
565	> `(bucket, tags…)` held until the scan ends — rather than the streaming operator. Index mode
566	> stays fully in scope (§2); it simply takes the safe path. Streaming is a part-path optimisation,
567	> and the plan must choose between them on `measureSchema.GetIndexMode()`, not on a runtime guess.
568	
569	The alternative — forcing a verified timestamp sort ahead of the operator for index mode — buys
570	back streaming at the cost of a blocking sort, which is what streaming existed to avoid. The map
571	is the honest trade.
572	
573	**The guard is not optional.** Streaming is correct *only* while the input is time-ordered. If
574	`orderByTS` were ever false on the part path, a bucket would be reopened after being flushed and
575	the query would emit duplicate rows for the same bucket — a silently wrong series, the exact
576	failure class this design exists to remove. Two defences, both required:
577	
578	1. **Analyzer** — reject (or refuse to stream) a bucketed request whose `order_by` resolves to
579	   anything other than time ordering, since that flips `orderByTS` to false.
580	2. **Operator** — assert monotonicity. A row whose bucket is *less* than the current bucket is an
581	   invariant violation; fail loudly rather than emit a second row for a closed bucket. This is one
582	   comparison per row and it converts a silent corruption into a loud error.
583	
584	Everything else downstream is unchanged: `keyIndices` gains the timestamp column index,
585	`computeKey` encodes it, `newGroup` copies it with the existing `copyOneValue`, and every row in
586	a group shares the bucket by construction.
587	
588	Three further consequences to handle:
589	
590	- **Reverse D2 conditionally.** `buildAggOutputLayout` (`aggregation.go:659`) must re-emit the
591	  `RoleTimestamp` column when — and only when — a bucket key is present. Today it never does, and
592	  `plan/build_test.go:221` asserts that; the assertion stays correct for the unbucketed case and
593	  gains a bucketed sibling. The serializer then populates `DataPoint.timestamp` from it, which is
594	  why §5.2 needs no new column name.
595	- **Negative timestamps.** Go's `%` truncates toward zero, so `bucketStart` skews by one bucket
596	  for `ts < 0`. Measure timestamps are Unix milliseconds and the write path rejects
597	  non-positive ones, so this is unreachable — but the helper should floor correctly anyway
598	  rather than depend on a caller's invariant.
599	- **Bucket ≠ segment.** The bucket width is unrelated to `ResourceOpts.segment_interval`, which
600	  is an `IntervalRule` restricted to HOUR/DAY and governs physical segmentation, not query
601	  grouping. A bucket may span segments and a segment may contain many buckets; nothing in the
602	  scan needs to know.
603	
604	**Distributed.** The bucket is a pure function of a value already on the row, so each data node
605	floors independently and no coordination is needed. Node partials become per
606	`(bucket, tag group)`; the liaison reduce must key on the bucket too. Two seams:
607	`distributedGroupByTagNames` (`distributed.go:1131`) returns tag names only and needs to carry
608	the bucket flag, and `resolveKeyIndices` (`reduce.go:169`) resolves `RoleTag` columns only and
609	needs to resolve the `RoleTimestamp` column as the leading key.
610	
611	The streaming property survives the fan-out, because **every node emits buckets in ascending
612	order**, so the liaison holds N sorted streams rather than N unordered heaps. That makes the
613	reduce a k-way merge on the bucket key: a bucket closes as soon as every node has moved past it,
614	and the liaison's live state is one bucket's groups rather than the whole window's. The same
615	`buckets × tagGroups` blow-up is avoided on both sides.
616	
617	Node-side streaming is mandatory (it is where the scan-sized state lives). Liaison-side merging
618	is a refinement worth separating, and the distinction matters for what the design is allowed to
619	claim: the vec distributed path broadcasts and **collects every response before `executeAgg`**
620	(`distributed.go:471-476`, `:638`), so the encoded payload is already fully resident. Merging
621	saves the decoded group state, not the buffering.
622	
623	That is why §2's requirement is worded as *node-local* streaming. Calling the whole query
624	pipelined while the liaison buffers all frames would be false. Genuine end-to-end pipelining
625	would need ordered partial streams, a liaison k-way merge, and cancellation/backpressure plumbing
626	— a separate piece of work, not a property this design delivers. A correct first cut
627	hash-aggregates on `(bucket, tags…)` at the liaison, bounded by what the nodes chose to send.
628	
629	### 7.3 COUNT_DISTINCT on a single node
630	
631	A new `AggCountDistinct` function and a new `aggSlot` variant holding a set of encoded values,
632	keyed by `appendKeyComponent` — the same encoder the group key already uses, which covers every
633	target type the matrix admits.
634	
635	The set itself belongs in `pkg/query/aggregation` (a new `distinct.go`), keeping aggregation
636	semantics in the package that owns them; `aggregation_test.go
637	TestBatchAggregation_DelegatesToAggregationPackage` pins that convention.
638	
639	```go
640	// Distinct accumulates the distinct values of one group.
641	type Distinct interface {
642	    In(key []byte) (added bool) // added is true on first sight; it drives the memory charge
643	    Val() int64
644	    Reset()
645	}
646	```
647	
648	`NewMap`/`NewReduce` (`aggregation.go:62`, `:82`) should keep returning `errUnknownFunc` for
649	`COUNT_DISTINCT`. That is not an oversight but the mechanism by which a `COUNT_DISTINCT` TopN
650	rule is rejected: `banyand/measure/topn_post_processor.go:285` calls `NewMap` and propagates the
651	error rather than mis-aggregating.
652	### 7.4 COUNT_DISTINCT across data nodes
653	
654	Every other function pushes down cleanly: the node reduces to a scalar `Partial` and the liaison
655	combines. `COUNT_DISTINCT` appears to break that, because per-node counts cannot in general be
656	summed — the same value seen on two nodes would count twice.
657	
658	**But it can be pushed down whenever shard placement partitions the value space, and that is
659	decidable statically.** So `COUNT_DISTINCT` pushes down like everything else, and a request that
660	cannot be pushed down is **rejected at analyze time** rather than served by a second, costlier
661	mechanism.
662	
663	**The rejection is uniform across deployment shapes.** A standalone server has no sharding, so it
664	could serve every `COUNT_DISTINCT` correctly — and deliberately does not. The condition is
665	evaluated in the analyzer, which runs identically in both modes, so a query either works
666	everywhere or nowhere. The alternative would let a query pass in a single-node development
667	environment and fail on a cluster, which is a worse failure than never having supported it: the
668	rule *the target must be the entity* is only teachable if it holds unconditionally.
669	
670	#### The decomposability condition
671	
672	Shard placement is deterministic and value-derived, but the values it derives from are **the
673	effective routing key**, which is not always the entity. `Locate` computes an entity-based shard
674	and then *overrides* it with the sharding-key router when one is configured
675	(`pkg/partition/route.go:51-65`); the liaison installs both routes
676	(`discovery.go:93-111`, sharding-key locator at `:428-452`), and the write path picks between
677	them at `liaison/grpc/measure.go:176-181`.
678	
679	> **routingTags** = the measure's `sharding_key` when configured, otherwise its entity tags.
680	
681	This is a supported schema shape, not a rejected input: `CheckShardingKeySubset`
682	(`api/validate/validate.go:228-255`) returns nil for a single entity tag, and a subset failure is
683	logged as a *warning* during create/update (`metadata/schema/property/client.go:779-809`). The
684	repo's own fixtures carry one — `service_instance_float_metric.json` has entity
685	`[service_id, entity_id]` with sharding key `[service_id]`.
686	
687	Every row sharing a set of routing tag values lands on exactly one shard. If fixing the group key
688	and the distinct value pins *every* routing tag, that `(group, value)` pair can exist on only one
689	shard, the per-shard distinct sets for a group are **disjoint**, and disjoint cardinalities add:
690	
691	> **routingTags ⊆ groupByTags ∪ {target}** ⟹ per-shard counts are summable.
692	
693	**This is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one.** Fixed predicates in the query, or a
694	proven functional dependency between tags, can equally pin a routing tag that is not grouped. The
695	design does not model either, so some decomposable queries are rejected. That is a deliberate
696	product gate — see *Policy, not necessity* below — and it should not be described as a
697	mathematical boundary.
698	
699	**Why stating this over entity tags is wrong**, concretely: entity `{e}`, sharding key `{s}`, and
700	`COUNT_DISTINCT(e)` with no grouping on `s`. An entity-based rule accepts it because the target
701	*is* the entity. But the same `e` occurring under two `s` values routes to two shards, each
702	reporting a local count of 1, summing to 2 for one distinct entity.
703	
704	When the condition holds, each node computes its own exact distinct count per `(bucket, group)`
705	and emits **one int64** in the existing `Partial{Value}` shape; the liaison reduces with **SUM**.
706	No new wire type, no new partial shape, and the whole `AggModeMap` → `AggModeReduce` machinery is
707	reused verbatim: `COUNT_DISTINCT` is *"local distinct, global sum"*.
708	
709	#### Multi-stage requests are rejected
710	
711	`(stage, shard, group)` identity decides whether two partials are *replicas*. It does **not**
712	make stage-local distinct counts additive, and an earlier draft wrongly assumed it did.
713	
714	Shards partition the *value* space; stages partition *time* — and a distinct value crosses time.
715	Hot holds group `g` with target set `{e1}`, warm holds `g` with `{e1}`: the true whole-range
716	answer is 1, and summing stage-local cardinalities gives 2. No migration overlap or duplicate
717	timestamp is needed; the same target legitimately occurs at different times in different stages.
718	
719	**Bucketing does not rescue it, and the reason is worth recording.** It is tempting to argue that
720	because stages do not overlap in time, a bucket falls inside one stage. But that non-overlap is
721	not visible to the analyzer: `parseNodeSelector` (`dquery.go:161-189`) only builds *selectors* —
722	it produces no stage time windows — and segment selection is by overlapping physical segment
723	range and retention (`storage/segment.go:612-649`, `tsdb.go:277-299`), not by a query-time
724	lifecycle boundary. Bucket width alone is not proof of single-stage ownership.
725	
726	> **Therefore: reject every resolved multi-stage `COUNT_DISTINCT`, bucketed or not.** Resolve the
727	> requested stages — including the `DefaultStages` fallback, which may list several — and reject
728	> if more than one survives. Never silently drop a stage.
729	
730	Lifting this later requires all of: a per-output-bucket read-ownership invariant that is
731	*enforced and analyzer-visible*, stable effective routing, correct per-shard partials, and
732	replica dedup. Short of that, the alternative is a value-bearing union across stages with its own
733	memory budget — the fallback this design rejects on cost grounds elsewhere.
734	
735	A related caveat with the same shape: `ResourceOpts.ShardNum` can be changed by `UpdateGroup`
736	(`metadata/schema/property/client.go:976-989`). A pure node rebalance that preserves logical
737	shard ids is harmless, but a modulus change creates historical routing domains, and a single
738	*current* shard count does not prove which modulus the older selected parts were written under.
739	Treat unchanged `shard_num` over the queried range as an assumption to establish, not a given.
740	
741	#### The rule, and what it means in practice
742	
743	For the common SkyWalking shape the condition collapses to something easy to predict. Those
744	measures declare both entity and sharding key as the single `entity_id` tag — visible in this
745	repo's fixtures, e.g. `pkg/test/measure/testdata/measures/endpoint_resp_time_minute.json`:
746	
747	```json
748	"entity":       { "tag_names": ["entity_id"] },
749	"sharding_key": { "tag_names": ["entity_id"] },
750	"interval": "1m"
751	```
752	
753	With `routingTags = {entity_id}`, `COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` satisfies
754	`routingTags ⊆ groupBy ∪ {target}` for any grouping, and a distinct over a non-routing tag such
755	as `service_id` does not.
756	
757	**The shorthand "distinct over the entity is always supported" is wrong** and was removed: it
758	holds only when the routing key *is* the entity. A measure with a narrower sharding key —
759	entity `[service_id, entity_id]`, sharding key `[service_id]`, as in
760	`service_instance_float_metric.json` — behaves differently in both directions. There,
761	`COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` grouped by `service_id` is accepted because `{service_id}` is
762	covered, while an ungrouped `COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` is rejected. **Always evaluate the
763	condition against `routingTags`, never against a remembered rule about entities.**
764	
765	Applied to the motivating workload, whose measures route on `entity_id`:
766	
767	| Case | Shape | Outcome |
768	|---|---|---|
769	| Distinct api-keys for one user | `COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id) WHERE service_id = …` | ✅ pushed down |
770	| Distinct api-keys per user | `GROUP BY service_id, COUNT_DISTINCT(entity_id)` | ✅ pushed down |
771	| The same, per time bucket, single stage | `+ TIME_BUCKET(w)` | ✅ pushed down |
772	| Any of the above resolving to **more than one stage** | — | ❌ rejected |
773	| Distinct *models* per user, as modelled today | model is inside a serialized blob, not a tag | ❌ not expressible at any layer |
774	| Distinct models, with the model promoted to an entity | structurally identical to the api-key case | ✅ pushed down |
775	| "How many distinct users exist?" | `COUNT_DISTINCT(service_id)` — not a routing tag | ❌ rejected |
776	
777	Every case this workload expresses is pushed down, **provided it resolves to a single stage** —
778	which is now a live constraint on the deployment, not a footnote, since an empty `stages` falls
779	back to `DefaultStages` and that may list several.
780	
781	#### Why rejection rather than a fallback
782	
783	A fallback path — nodes shipping their distinct *values* for the liaison to union — is always
784	correct and needs no condition check. It was considered and rejected (§9), because:
785	
786	- **Its cost is unbounded and user-controlled.** Wire volume and liaison memory scale with
787	  cardinality, so one `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a high-cardinality tag funnels every value into a
788	  single process. "Slow and correct" is a poor trade when the liaison is shared infrastructure;
789	  the failure lands on every other query in flight.
790	- **It makes the cost model unpredictable.** Two queries that look alike would differ by orders
791	  of magnitude depending on a schema property the author cannot see in the query text. A hard
792	  rule — *the target must be the entity* — is something a user can reason about in advance.
793	- **It doubles the surface.** Two implementations of one function, a static chooser between them,
794	  opposite replica-dedup requirements (union is idempotent, summation is not), and a differential
795	  test to keep them honest — all to serve queries the data model says should be written
796	  differently.
797	- **It is inconsistent with the rest of this design**, which already rejects rather than
798	  approximates: array and timestamp tags (§6), numeric functions over string tags (§6), bucket
799	  a bucket width with no source to resolve it from (§5.3), tag aggregation on the row engine (§8).
800	
801	Rejection is also the honest signal. A `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a non-entity tag is usually a
802	modelling mismatch, and the error should say so rather than silently serving it expensively:
803	
804	```
805	count_distinct(service_id) is not supported: the target must be part of the measure's
806	entity (entity_id), or every entity tag must appear in GROUP BY. Either group by
807	service_id and count_distinct(entity_id), or model service_id as an entity tag.
808	```
809	
810	The user is not stuck: `GROUP BY <target>` and counting the returned rows client-side still
811	works exactly as it does today, and is the same shape the fallback would have implemented — only
812	with the cost visible to the caller who chose it.
813	
814	#### Policy, not necessity
815	
816	Three of the rejections above are **product decisions and should be read as such**, not as
817	mathematical boundaries:
818	
819	- The condition is *sufficient*, not necessary. Fixed predicates and proven functional
820	  dependencies could pin an ungrouped routing tag; this design models neither.
821	- Grouping by every effective routing tag can make a **non-routing target** decomposable. Such
822	  queries are rejected because the analyzer does not reason about it, not because they are
823	  unanswerable.
824	- Rejecting uniformly in standalone (§7.4) forgoes queries a single node could union locally and
825	  exactly. That is a portability choice — one contract regardless of deployment shape — and is
826	  only defensible while it is stated deliberately rather than presented as a limit of the maths.
827	
828	Each is a place where the engine could later do more without changing any wire format. Recording
829	them as policy keeps that door visible; describing them as necessity would quietly close it.
830	
831	#### De-duplicating the partials
832	
833	Replicas of a shard hold identical data, so selecting one copy per replica set is the right
834	mechanism. It needs two fixes to be correct, because today's deduped unit is neither a shard nor
835	a stage.
836	
837	**(a) Today's partial is per-node, and its shard label is a hint.** `computeKey`
838	(`aggregation.go:523`) builds the group key from `keyIndices` — the group-by tags only — and
839	`newGroup` stamps the group with the shard id of the *first row that created it*. A node holding
840	shards 1 and 2 emits **one** partial for group `g` covering both, labelled with whichever shard
841	appeared first. "The replicas are all the same" is true of shards and not of these partials.
842	
843	Within a node each shard appears exactly once — there are no duplicate shards on a node — so a
844	per-shard partial is always well defined. That property is what makes the fix below *correct*;
845	it is not what makes today's labelling *sufficient*. What breaks today is that node shard-*sets*
846	differ, and under replication they do, by construction:
847	
848	```go
849	// pkg/node/round_robin.go:218
850	func (r *roundRobinSelector) selectNode(index int, replicasID uint32) string {
851		adjustedIndex := index + int(replicasID)
852		return r.nodes[adjustedIndex%len(r.nodes)]
853	}
854	```
855	
856	Placement is *staggered*, so with 4 nodes, 4 shards and `replicas=1`:
857	
858	| | shard 0 | shard 1 | shard 2 | shard 3 |
859	|---|---|---|---|---|
860	| replica 0 | n0 | n1 | n2 | n3 |
861	| replica 1 | n1 | n2 | n3 | n0 |
862	
863	giving `n0={s0,s3}`, `n1={s0,s1}`, `n2={s1,s2}`, `n3={s2,s3}`. No node holds a shard twice, every

942	#### Composition and touch points
943	
944	`groupKeys` above is whatever §7.2 produced — with `time_bucket` set it is `[bucket] ++ tagKeys`,
945	so the bucket is just another leading key column and the two features compose without a special
946	case. Push-down composes especially well with the streaming design: the node's distinct set is
947	released when a bucket closes, so it emits a scalar per `(bucket, group)` and never holds more
948	than one bucket's values.
949	
950	Touch points: `distributedAggFunc` (`:1142`) gains an entry mapping `COUNT_DISTINCT` to the
951	existing SUM reducer; `BuildOperators` (`plan.go:61`) builds the local distinct slot in the map
952	phase and adds the shard to `keyIndices`; `markDedupSeen` takes the stage; the analyzer gains the
953	condition check and its rejection. `nodeTemplate.Limit` is already `MaxUint32` whenever
954	`Agg != nil` (`:222`), which remains harmless here since partials are per-group scalars.
955	### 7.5 Ranking, ordering and paging
956	
957	**Ranking is unchanged.** `ApplyTopToReduce` (`reduce.go:290`) resolves `RoleField && Name ==
958	top.FieldName` on the reduced batch, and the aggregate result is exactly such a column;
959	`offset`/`limit` are applied by `iteratorFromBatches` (`distributed.go:988`). The ranked case
960	therefore falls out of §7.4 with no extra work.
961	
962	**Node-local ordering needs no sort pass — but that is the only place it's free.** Because §7.2
963	streams buckets in ascending order, and `BatchAggregation` already emits groups in insertion
964	order (`BatchAggregation.insertion`), one node's own bucketed output is bucket-ascending by
965	construction, with no extra pass. This is the second dividend of streaming: a sort over
966	`buckets × tagGroups` rows would have been cheap in absolute terms but would have re-imposed a
967	blocking stage on an otherwise pipelined query, forfeiting the latency win. The third dividend is
968	that the bucket-advance check this operator already performs is exactly the span boundary
969	run-folding needs (§7.7).
970	
971	**An earlier version of this section claimed the liaison merge and index mode inherit that same
972	ordering "by construction." They do not, and implementing §7.2 surfaced both gaps:**
973	
974	- **The liaison reduce.** `ReducePartialBatches` consumes each node's partial fully before moving
975	  to the next, so `BatchAggregation.insertion` ends up only *piecewise* ascending — node A's
976	  `[2000, 3000]` followed by node B's `[1000, 2000]` inserts as `[2000, 3000, 1000]`, not merged.
977	  `iteratorFromBatches`'s offset/limit pagination needs the globally merged order, not the
978	  per-partial one.
979	- **Index mode's map fallback.** §7.2's non-streaming path holds one persistent aggregator across
980	  the whole scan precisely because its input may not be time-ordered — so its insertion order is
981	  first-seen, not bucket order, by design.
982	
983	Both are fixed the same way: `BatchAggregation.SortInsertionByBucket()` stable-sorts
984	`a.insertion` by each group's captured bucket timestamp immediately before it is drained (once in
985	`ReducePartialBatches`, after `Finalize`; once in `BatchTimeBucket`'s map-mode terminal drain). It
986	is a no-op for a streaming-mode instance, since every group in one such instance already shares
987	the same bucket by construction — so the fix costs nothing on the already-correct path and only
988	does real work where ordering was not actually free. **Any future aggregate that reuses this
989	reduce path (COUNT_DISTINCT included — see §7.4, which pushes down through the same
990	`AggModeMap`/`AggModeReduce` machinery) inherits this fix automatically and must not re-introduce
991	the "ordering is free" assumption.**
992	
993	Ordering and `top` interact in the obvious way — `top` selects globally (§3), then the surviving
994	rows are emitted in bucket order. A client wanting "the global top 20 devices, plotted over time"
995	gets exactly that; a client wanting per-bucket top-N wants the TopN RPC.
996	
997	### 7.6 Memory safety
998	
999	A distinct set grows with cardinality, unlike the fixed-size numeric slots, so it must be charged
1000	**per inserted value**, not per group. `BatchAggregation.Consume` already reserves `entrySize`
1001	per new group from the shared `MemoryTracker` (`aggregation.go:326-333`); the distinct path
1002	additionally reserves on each `added` value and refunds the total in `Close`. A high-cardinality
1003	target then fails with the existing `"aggregation memory budget exceeded"` message against the
1004	256 MiB default (`VectorizedConfig.QueryMemoryMiB`).
1005	
1006	**This also requires fixing `reduce.go:133`, which passes `entrySize=0`** — the liaison reduce is
1007	unbudgeted today. That is tolerable for scalar partials and not tolerable for sets, since the
1008	liaison is exactly where the union of every node's distinct values lands. Note this is a
1009	**node-side** concern specifically. Because §7.4 pushes down, the liaison holds no sets at all —
1010	one int64 per `(stage, shard, group)` — so the sets that need charging live only on the nodes,
1011	where the scan-sized state already is.
1012	
1013	**Time bucketing does not multiply the live group count**, because §7.2 streams: a bucketed query
1014	holds one bucket's groups, not `buckets × tagGroups`. This is the main reason the streaming shape
1015	matters rather than being a mere optimisation — the naive map would have made a 24-hour/1-minute
1016	query cost 1440× the unbucketed group count, and for `COUNT_DISTINCT` each of those 1440× groups
1017	would have held its own set.
1018	
1019	What bucketing *does* change is the shape of the peak: the live set is now the widest single
1020	bucket rather than the whole window. A bucket with pathological cardinality still fails the
1021	budget, and that is the correct outcome — but it fails on one bucket's data, which is both a
1022	smaller number and a far more interpretable error than "the query as a whole was too big".
1023	
1024	Two bounds keep this defensible:
1025	
1026	- **Per bucket**, live groups ≤ distinct `(tags…)` in that bucket ≤ rows in that bucket. The
1027	  aggregation can never hold more than the scan hands it for the bucket it is on.
1028	- **Across the window**, bucket count is `time_range / width`. Streaming means that no longer
1029	  governs memory, but it still governs *output* rows, which is what `limit` must accommodate
1030	  (§10). A very small width against a long window is therefore a paging problem rather than a
1031	  memory one.
1032	
1033	---
1034	
1035	### 7.7 The local scan: entity and indexed tags never touch the data file
1036	
1037	A `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a tag, grouped by a bucket and other tags, can in the common case be
1038	answered **without decoding a single tag column** — because the tag values are already resident
1039	from the series index, and the only thing the scan needs from the part is which series appear in
1040	which bucket.
1041	
1042	**The projection is split before the data file is reached.** `searchSeriesList`
1043	(`query.go:314-356`) sorts every requested tag into one of three buckets:
1044	
1045	| Tag kind | Resolved from | Reaches the block cursor? |
1046	|---|---|---|
1047	| **Entity tag** | `projectedEntityOffsets` → `SeriesList[].EntityValues` (`query.go:486-493`) | **no** — `continue TAG` |
1048	| **Indexed tag** (`is.fieldIndexLocation`) | `indexProjection` → the series index `fieldResult` | **no** — `continue TAG` |
1049	| anything else | the part's tag columns | yes, via `newTagProjection` |
1050	
1051	Only the third category is appended to `newTagProjection`, and only `newTagProjection` becomes
1052	`bc.tagProjection`. So `unmarshalTagFamily` never reads a column for an entity or indexed tag,
1053	and `copyAllTo` (`block.go:535-552`) takes the value from `indexValue[tagName]` and skips the
1054	block column outright. Both kinds are series-scoped — one value replicated across the block's
1055	rows — which is precisely why they can live outside the data file at all.
1056	
1057	**What a pure index-resolved aggregation actually reads** — valid only when *every* required tag
1058	(group keys, aggregation target, and any tag a residual predicate touches) resolves from the
1059	series index. One part-resident tag anywhere in the query reinstates the `.tfm`/`.tf` reads for
1060	its family, so this is a property of the whole query, not of the aggregation target alone:
1061	
1062	| File | Read? |
1063	|---|---|
1064	| `sidx/` (series index) | once per segment — series list plus projected index values |
1065	| `meta.bin` | at part open only; the primary-block index stays resident |
1066	| `primary.bin` | selectively, per matching series |
1067	| `timestamps.bin` | per block — but see below |
1068	| `<family>.tfm` / `.tf` | **never** |
1069	| `field.bin` | **never** — this query shape projects no field |
1070	
1071	**It goes one step further than "metadata plus timestamps".** `blockMetadata` carries
1072	`seriesID`, `timestamps.min`, `timestamps.max` and `count`, all resident after
1073	`readPrimaryBlock` with no data-file read. When `bucketOf(min) == bucketOf(max)` the whole block
1074	lies inside one bucket, so the series' presence in that bucket is known from metadata alone and
1075	`timestamps.bin` need not be read either — **but only if the block is also fully contained in the
1076	query's time range**. Block selection is range-*aware*, not range-*clipped*: it returns any block
1077	whose `[min,max]` overlaps the requested range (`query.go:594-629`). A block with rows at 09:00
1078	and 09:59 occupies a single hourly bucket, yet a query for 09:30–09:31 matches neither row.
1079	Testing `bucketOf(min) == bucketOf(max)` alone would report a bucket that has no matching data. The scan degenerates to:
1080	
1081	```
1082	for each block matching (series filter, time range):
1083	    group key  ← seriesID → routing tag values      (series index, already in hand)
1084	    bucket(s)  ← [min,max] ONLY IF the block is fully inside the query range
1085	                 AND min/max share a bucket AND no residual predicate can exclude rows;
1086	                 otherwise read timestamps.bin and filter
1087	    count distinct seriesID per (bucket, group)
1088	```
1089	
1090	All three conditions are required. Dropping the containment check reports empty buckets;
1091	dropping the predicate check reports buckets whose rows are all filtered out.
1092	
1093	For `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a tag that is **functionally determined by the series** — an entity
1094	tag, which every series pins by construction — this is exact by identity: counting distinct
1095	values *is* counting distinct series, and a series either appears in a bucket or it does not. It
1096	does **not** extend to an arbitrary index-resolved tag: an indexed non-entity tag is
1097	series-constant, so it is still readable without the data file, but several series may share a
1098	value, and the count must then go through the distinct set rather than the series count.
1099	
1100	Four things bound the optimisation, and they should be settled before it is built:
1101	
1102	- **Straddling *or* partially-selected blocks still need `timestamps.bin`.** A block spanning
1103	  09:00–11:00 with no rows in the 10:00 bucket must not report presence there, so `[min,max]`
1104	  cannot be over-approximated into a bucket range; and a block only partly inside the query range
1105	  must be filtered rather than assumed present. How much the shortcut actually buys therefore
1106	  depends on bucket width against block span *and* on how often a block sits wholly inside the
1107	  requested range — which is why the payoff is worth measuring before this stage is built rather
1108	  than assumed from the bucket width alone.
1109	- **It applies to `COUNT` and `COUNT_DISTINCT` only.** `SUM`/`MIN`/`MAX`/`MEAN` over a field
1110	  obviously need field data, and over a non-entity, non-indexed tag any function needs the tag
1111	  column.
1112	- **`blockMetadata.count` is not a row count for `COUNT`.** It counts stored entries including
1113	  superseded versions, while the query path dedups `(seriesID, timestamp)` keeping the highest
1114	  version (`queryResult.merge`). Using it directly would over-count duplicates. The identity
1115	  holds for distinct-series counting, which is version-insensitive, and fails for row counting —
1116	  a sharp distinction worth encoding in a test.
1117	- **It is a separate execution strategy, not a tweak.** The pipeline today decodes blocks into
1118	  `MeasureResult` rows and feeds the vec operators; this bypasses block decode entirely. Bounded
1119	  work, but a new path with its own correctness surface — so it belongs after the main design
1120	  lands, gated on a differential test against the decoding path.
1121	
1122	#### Intermediate step: fold by run, not by row
1123	
1124	The metadata-only scan above is the end state. There is a cheaper step on the way to it that
1125	needs **no new execution strategy at all**, only a change inside the aggregation operator — and
1126	it removes most of the same waste.
1127	
1128	An index-resolved tag is series-constant, but nothing downstream knows that, so the single value
1129	is multiplied out three times before it is folded:
1130	
1131	1. **Replicated.** `copyAllTo` expands one value into `n` pointers —
1132	   `for i := 0; i < size; i++ { t.Values[i] = indexValue[tagName] }`.
1133	2. **Materialised.** `appendTagValueAsTyped` appends it into the native column one row at a time,
1134	   so the column physically holds `n` entries of the same value.
1135	3. **Folded.** `BatchAggregation.Consume` is row-oriented: per row it calls `computeKey`, probes
1136	   `a.groups[key]`, and folds. `computeKey` ends in `return string(buf)`, and that string is
1137	   stored in the group map, so it escapes — **a heap allocation per row**. Go's
1138	   `m[string(b)]` no-allocation optimisation does not apply across the function boundary.
1139	
1140	So a block costs `n` × {key encode, string allocation, map hash + probe + compare, fold}, and
1141	from the second row onward every one of those reproduces an identical result. For
1142	`COUNT_DISTINCT` the `n−1` redundant set inserts are idempotent no-ops that still pay a hash and
1143	a probe each. `n` here is rows per series per block, bounded by `maxBlockLength = 8192`
1144	(`banyand/measure/measure.go:46`).
1145	
1146	**Two facts make run-folding almost free to add:**
1147	
1148	- **A batch is single-series.** `BuildMeasureBatchFromResult` consumes exactly one
1149	  `model.MeasureResult`, and `queryResult.merge` returns as soon as the seriesID changes — so
1150	  `seriesID` never varies inside a batch and needs no checking.
1151	- **§7.2 already finds the boundaries.** The streaming operator walks the timestamp column
1152	  looking for bucket advances. Because input is timestamp-ascending and the series is fixed, the
1153	  rows form *contiguous* spans of constant `(series, bucket)` — and a bucket advance is exactly a
1154	  span boundary. The detection is already there; only the folding is per-row.
1155	
1156	**The change:** for each maximal span sharing `(series, bucket)`, compute the key once, resolve
1157	the group once, and fold the span in one operation.
1158	
1159	| Aggregate | Per span |
1160	|---|---|
1161	| `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a series-constant target | **one** set insert |
1162	| `COUNT` | `count += spanLength` |
1163	| `SUM` / `MIN` / `MAX` / `MEAN` over a varying column | still per row — but the key work is saved |
1164	
1165	**Magnitude.** 8192 rows of 1-minute data is roughly 5.7 days inside one block; at hour buckets
1166	that is about 137 spans, so 8192 key computations, allocations and map probes collapse to ~137.
1167	Unbucketed, 8192 collapses to 1.
1168	
1169	**What it needs:** a plan-time flag marking which key columns are index-resolved, which
1170	`searchSeriesList`'s three-way split already determines — the information exists, it simply is
1171	not carried forward today. Correctness rests on the series-constancy guarantee, so the flag must
1172	be derived from that split rather than inferred by sampling column values at runtime; a column
1173	that merely *happens* to be constant in one batch must not take this path.
1174	
1175	Ordering relative to §7.7's metadata-only scan: this step is strictly cheaper than today, strictly
1176	simpler than the metadata-only scan, and the two are compatible — run-folding helps every
1177	aggregation whose keys are index-resolved, including the ones that still have to read a part-file
1178	column for the aggregate itself, which the metadata-only path cannot serve at all.
1179	
1180	**`index_mode` measures are this section's structural case.** They hold no part-resident tags at
1181	all — `buildIndexQueryResult` errors on any projected tag that is neither an entity offset nor an
1182	indexed field — so an index-mode aggregation is index-only by construction rather than by
1183	fortunate schema design. Two consequences: the `.tf`/`.tfm` rows of the table above do not merely
1184	go unread, they do not exist; and the "straddling blocks" bound does not apply, since there are
1185	no data blocks to straddle. Index mode should therefore be the first place the metadata-only path
1186	is built and measured.
1187	
1188	Note the asymmetry with §7.2: index mode is the *best* case for scan cost and the *worst* case
1189	for ordering, since it bypasses the timestamp-ordering default entirely. It reads least and
1190	streams least.
1191	
1192	One caveat for run-folding specifically: index mode materialises one row per index entry
1193	(`copyTo` builds a single-timestamp `MeasureResult`), so the multi-row single-series batch that
1194	run-folding collapses may not arise on that path. Run-folding targets the part-file scan; the
1195	batch-oriented `PullBatch` path for index mode should be checked before assuming it benefits.
1196	
1197	This is also an argument for the §7.4 modelling guidance from the other direction: putting the
1198	distinct target in the routing key does not merely make the query *pushable*, it makes the local
1199	scan metadata-only.
1200

1222	## 9. Alternatives considered
1223	
1224	| Alternative | Why rejected |
1225	|---|---|
1226	| **Aggregate inside the native inverted index** | The engine already aggregates locally on data nodes, so this would not reduce network cost — it only moves which layer owns local aggregation, while duplicating grouping, arithmetic, memory accounting and distributed reduction. Estimated 5–8+ engineer-weeks against 2–4 for extending the engine. |
1227	| **HyperLogLog partials** | Constant wire cost and no decomposability condition to check, but it needs a new partial wire type and an API contract about error bounds. §7.4 already gets cardinality-independent wire *exactly* whenever the condition holds, which covers the motivating shape — so a sketch would buy only the queries §7.4 rejects, and would buy them approximately. That is the right thing to revisit if those rejections turn out to matter, and the wrong thing to build speculatively. |
1228	| **A value-shipping fallback** for queries that fail the condition — nodes ship distinct values, liaison unions | Always correct and needs no condition check, but its wire volume and liaison memory scale with cardinality, so a single query can funnel every value into shared infrastructure. It also doubles the surface: two implementations, a static chooser, opposite replica-dedup requirements, and a differential test to keep them honest. Rejecting is consistent with how this design treats every other unsupported shape. §7.4. |
1229	| **Ship per-node counts and sum them** | Wrong. A value appearing on two nodes is counted twice; that is the same class of bug as the multi-bucket `COUNT(*)` this design removes. |
1230	| **Emit an explicit set-typed partial column** | Same wire volume as shipping distinct tuples, but needs a new column type, a new frame wire type, and a new `Partial` shape. Reusing the group-by shape costs nothing extra. |
1231	| **Solve it upstream instead** — change SkyWalking to store labelled metric values as tags | An OAP core change touching all three storage plugins, and it multiplies row count by label cardinality — the packed representation exists precisely to prevent that. Out of scope here regardless, since it does not remove the need for `COUNT_DISTINCT`. |
1232	| **Requiring the width to be a multiple of `Measure.interval`** | Rejected after the fact that motivated it turned out not to hold: `interval` is a declared write cadence, not a storage invariant, so data points do not reliably land on interval boundaries. With arbitrary timestamps every width bins just as meaningfully as any other, and the rule would refuse useful queries to protect an alignment that was never guaranteed. §5.3. |
1233	| **A `multiplier` integer instead of a duration string** | Makes invalid widths unrepresentable, but `multiplier: 5` cannot be read without the measure schema in hand — it means 5 minutes or 5 hours depending on the measure. A duration string matches `Measure.interval`'s own encoding, parses with the same helper, and matches the `INTERVAL <width>` spelling the bucketing functions in §1 use. Validation is one modulo. |
1234	| **Bucket on `segment_interval`** rather than `Measure.interval` | `ResourceOpts.segment_interval` is an `IntervalRule` restricted to HOUR/DAY and describes physical segmentation, not data-point cadence. It is both too coarse and semantically unrelated. |
1235	| **Hash-map the bucket** — add it to `keyIndices` and hold every `(bucket, tags…)` until the scan ends | The path of least resistance, and wrong for a time-series database. It holds `buckets × tagGroups` live groups (1440× for a day at 1-minute), blocks all output until the last row, and then needs a sort to restore time order — all three paid for information the scan already provides, since measure results arrive timestamp-ascending by default (`query.go:286`). §7.2 streams instead. |
1236	| **Reuse the TopN RPC for series** | `TopNResponse.lists` is already a per-timestamp series, but the RPC ranks a single pre-aggregated field by a pre-declared `TopNAggregation` rule. It cannot express an ad-hoc `COUNT_DISTINCT` over a tag, and it requires schema registration ahead of the query. |

1240	## 10. Compatibility and follow-ups
1241	
1242	- **Wire.** All three API additions are additive. Old clients never set `tag_name` or
1243	  `time_bucket`, and never receive a `COUNT_DISTINCT` response.
1244	- **No new configuration.** `COUNT_DISTINCT` either pushes down or the request is rejected, so
1245	  there is no flag, no default to choose and no second path to keep warm. The §7.4 per-shard
1246	  partial ships as part of that single path rather than behind a gate, and is correct on its own
1247	  terms; only the question of whether it *also* fixes a live defect in `SUM`/`COUNT` is deferred
1248	  to the parallel experiment.
1249	- **Mixed-version clusters.** A liaison that sends a `COUNT_DISTINCT` request to an older data
1250	  node gets the node's existing unknown-function error rather than a wrong number, because
1251	  `protoAggFuncToInternal` (`plan.go:167`) rejects enum values it does not know. **`time_bucket`
1252	  has no such guard** — an old node silently ignores the unknown proto field and returns
1253	  whole-range partials, which the liaison would otherwise reduce into one row per tag group with
1254	  no error: a series collapsed to a point, silently.
1255	
1256	  The check is **self-describing**, needing no capability negotiation. A bucketed query's partial
1257	  carries a `RoleTimestamp` column, because §7.2 reverses D2 exactly when a bucket key is
1258	  present. A node that ignored the field emits partials *without* that column, so the liaison
1259	  detects the absence directly and hard-errors. This is deliberately not a node-version or
1260	  capability lookup: `database.v1.Node` carries only `metadata`, `roles`, addresses and a generic
1261	  `labels` map, so no such mechanism exists to consult — and inventing one to answer a question
1262	  the data already answers would be the wrong trade.
1263	- **`limit` with a bucketed query.** Result rows are `buckets × tagGroups`, so the default

1264	  `limit` of 100 (`measure_analyzer.go:32 defaultLimit`) truncates a 1-hour/1-minute/50-device
1265	  series at 100 of its 3000 rows. The default is left alone — changing it would alter unbucketed
1266	  queries too — but clients must set `limit` explicitly, and this needs to be prominent in the
1267	  BydbQL docs rather than buried in the API reference.
1268	- **Possible follow-up: multiple aggregates, then aliases.** Out of scope here by decision (§3),
1269	  and recorded only so the route stays visible if the remainder of §1.1 is ever wanted.
1270	  `AggSpec` is already a slice and `BatchAggregation` already loops over `a.aggs`, so the
1271	  constraint is the singular `QueryRequest.agg` field and BydbQL's one-aggregate rule — API and
1272	  planning, not execution. Aliases need a BydbQL `AS` production and an
1273	  `Aggregation.output_name` field together, and the two share one question: what a result column
1274	  is called when there is more than one.
1275	- **Follow-up: per-bucket `top`.** If demand appears, the honest move is to extend the TopN RPC
1276	  rather than overload `QueryRequest.top`, since TopN already returns a per-timestamp series.
1277	- **Follow-up: gap filling.** Needs a declared bucket set and a zero value per aggregate; SUM and
1278	  COUNT fill with 0, MIN/MAX/MEAN have no defensible fill.
1279	
1280	### Fixed: adjacent inconsistency in the liaison-side key resolution
1281	
1282	`reduce.go resolveKeyIndices` used to match key tags by `Name` only, ignoring `TagFamily`, unlike
1283	`plan.go:140` and `distributed.go:945`, which both compare the family. An earlier version of
1284	this note claimed that was safe because "tag names are unique per measure" — that directly
1285	contradicts §5.1 above, which debunks exactly that assumption (tag-family validation does not
1286	reject a name repeated across families, and `pkg/query/vectorized/schema_test.go` exercises it
1287	as a valid case). A bucketed or tag-keyed distributed reduce over such a schema could silently
1288	bind to the wrong family's column. Fixed by threading the key's `TagFamily` alongside its names
1289	end to end — `distributedGroupByTagKey` (`distributed.go`) now returns `(family, names)` instead
1290	of discarding the family, and `resolveKeyIndices` matches on `(family, name)`, same as `plan.go`
1291	and `distributed.go`'s row-merge path.

1318	  mis-evaluated condition does not crash — it returns an inflated count that looks entirely
1319	  plausible. There is no fallback path to diff against, so the tests must pin the predicate
1320	  directly and pin the rejection.
1321	  - **Accept/reject table over schemas**, driven by `routingTags` not entity tags:
1322	    `routingTags ⊆ groupBy ∪ target` (accept); a routing tag in neither (reject); `index_mode`

1325	  - **The sharding-key counterexample**, which an entity-based rule accepts and must not: entity
1326	    `{e}`, sharding key `{s}`, rows carrying the same `e` under two `s` values, and
1327	    `COUNT_DISTINCT(e)` with no grouping on `s`. Must reject. Summing scalar partials here
1328	    returns 2 for one distinct entity.
1329	  - **Multi-stage rejection**: the same query must be rejected when the resolved stage set has
1330	    more than one entry, bucketed or not — and the resolution must expand `DefaultStages`, not
1331	    only an explicit `stages` list. Pair it with the positive case: the same target in two
1332	    *disjoint buckets* of a single stage must count once per bucket and must **not** be rejected
1333	    for that reason.
1334	  - **Ambiguous tag name**: two families each containing `region`; an aggregation naming `region`
1335	    must resolve by its family qualifier, and an unqualified reference must fail naming both
1336	    families rather than silently binding to whichever family `RegisterTag` wrote last.
1337	  - **The rejection is a contract, not an implementation detail.** Assert the error is returned
1338	    at analyze time, before any node is contacted, and that its text names the target, the
1339	    entity, and the two ways out. A test on the message is warranted here because the message is
1340	    the entire remediation path for a user who has hit it.
1341	  - **An overlapping fixture must be rejected, not silently summed**: the same distinct value
1342	    present on two shards for one group. This is precisely the data shape that makes push-down
1343	    wrong, so what is under test is that the condition catches it rather than that the arithmetic
1344	    handles it.
1345	  - **Replica duplication must be deduped**: feed the same `(stage, shard, group)` partial twice
1346	    and assert the count does not double. Then feed two partials differing only in shard, and
1347	    assert they *do* add — the two halves of §7.4(c), which fail in opposite directions.
1348	  - **Standalone/distributed agreement**: the same query and fixture must return the same number
1349	    single-node and across nodes. Single-node has no sharding, so this is the cheapest end-to-end
1350	    check that the partition arithmetic is right.
1351	  - **Replicated-topology agreement** (§7.4): the same query and fixture must return the same
1352	    number at `replicas=0` and `replicas=1`. This is the regression test the per-shard partial

1356	  - `bucketStart` agrees with `getWindowStart` (`sliding_window.go:302`) across a table of

1360	  - `plan/build_test.go:221` currently asserts the output schema drops the timestamp. That

1363	    conditional rather than repealed.
1364	  - **`COUNT` and `COUNT_DISTINCT` must be allowed to disagree at the interval width.** An

1366	    `Measure.interval`, on the belief that storage holds one row per `(entity, bucket)`. It does

1368	    legal data. Invert it: seed one entity with two off-cadence points inside one bucket

1395	**Integration** — `test/cases/measure/`
1396	
1397	Cases are `input/<name>.yaml` + `input/<name>.ql` + golden `want/<name>.yaml`, registered as a
1398	`g.Entry` in `measure.go`; `data.go verifyQLWithRequest` proto-compares the QL transform against

1400	
1401	The load-bearing case is a **multi-bucket cardinality fixture**: one user with 3 api-keys spread
1402	across 3 hour buckets, a second user with 2, asserting `3` and `2` for the scalar case and the
1403	correct ordering for the ranked, paged case. It must run in the **distributed** suite
1404	(`test/integration/distributed/query/vectorized_test.go`, liaison + 2 data nodes) as well as
1405	standalone — the cross-node union has no single-node analogue, and a fixture confined to one
1406	bucket is exactly what lets the naive `COUNT(*)` over-count slip through unnoticed.
1407	
1408	The same fixture serves the series case at a second bucket width, and that is the point of
1409	reusing it: at a 1-hour bucket the same data must yield one row per `(hour, user)` whose counts
1410	sum to neither 3 nor 2, while at whole-range it must yield exactly 3 and 2. A fixture that only
1411	ever asks one width cannot catch a bucket key that is computed but ignored.
1412	
1413	**The decisive test for bucketing is a single-bucket decomposition check.** The oracle is
1414	constructed *by the test*, not borrowed from any client: a bucketed query over a window must
1415	equal the union of one-bucket-wide queries over the same window, because each of those is exact
1416	by the storage invariant (§1, workaround 1).
1417	
1418	```
1419	for each bucket B in window:                        one bucketed query over the window
1420	    query(time_range = B, group_by = tags)    ==    (group_by = TIME_BUCKET(w), tags)
1421	```
1422	
1423	Run both against the same fixture and compare row-for-row, keyed by `(bucket, tags…)`. This is
1424	worth more than any hand-written golden file, because each single-bucket query is independently
1425	trustworthy — it is the one shape the engine already answers exactly — so the comparison has a
1426	real oracle rather than a recorded expectation. It catches the whole class of off-by-one
1427	bucket-boundary errors that a golden file would simply enshrine. It also gives any caller
1428	currently issuing per-bucket queries a migration check they can run themselves before switching
1429	to a single bucketed query.
1430	
1431	Golden files must be **timestamp-stable**. `data.go` ignores timestamps when comparing, which is
1432	precisely the field a bucketed result asserts on, so these cases need the comparison to include
1433	it — otherwise the suite would pass with every bucket collapsed to zero.
1434	
1435	**Manual**
1436	
1437	```sql
1438	-- Scalar case — one user, 3 buckets. Must return 3, not 6.
1439	SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) FROM MEASURE … WHERE service_id = '<user>' TIME > '-3h';
1440	
1441	-- Ranked case — all users, ranked, paged.
1442	SELECT service_id, COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) FROM MEASURE … TIME > '-3h'
1443	GROUP BY service_id ORDER BY entity_id DESC LIMIT 20;
1444	
1445	-- Series case — one row per (5-minute bucket, host).
1446	SELECT host, COUNT(host) FROM MEASURE … TIME > '-1h'
1447	GROUP BY TIME_BUCKET('5m'), host LIMIT 1000;
1448	```

18	// Package plan is the vectorized measure-query plan tree (G8).
19	//
20	// Top-level dispatch (banyand/query/processor.go, G8d) routes every
21	// measure query here.
22	//
23	// A VecPlan node knows its output BatchSchema, its children, and how to
24	// append itself to a *vectorized.PipelineBuilder during Build. Build is
25	// bottom-up: a node calls Build on its child first, then attaches its own
26	// operator. The root's Build returns a fully-composed PipelineBuilder
27	// that the executor (G8c) finalizes via builder.Build() to produce a
28	// *vectorized.Pipeline.
29	package plan
30	
31	import (
32		"context"
33	
34		"github.com/apache/skywalking-banyandb/pkg/query/vectorized"
35		measure "github.com/apache/skywalking-banyandb/pkg/query/vectorized/measure"
36	)
37	
38	// VecPlan is the vectorized measure-query plan node interface.
39	//
40	// Schema returns the BatchSchema of rows this node emits — for fusible
41	// or schema-preserving breakers it matches the input schema; for
42	// schema-rewriting breakers (BatchAggregation) it is the operator's
43	// OutputSchema.
44	//
45	// Children returns the immediate child plan nodes (zero for leaves).
46	//
47	// Build appends this node's contribution to bc.Builder. The leaf (Scan)
48	// calls Builder.From; fusible nodes call Builder.Apply; breakers call
49	// Builder.Break. Build must call Build on its children before attaching
50	// itself so the source flows in tree order.
51	//
52	// String returns a single-line debug description ("Scan(measure=foo)",
53	// "GroupByAgg(keys=svc, fn=sum, field=value)", etc.) so plan trees can be
54	// pretty-printed with PrintTree.
55	type VecPlan interface {
56		Schema() *vectorized.BatchSchema
57		Children() []VecPlan
58		Build(ctx context.Context, bc *BuildContext) error
59		String() string
60	}
61	
62	// BuildContext is the cross-cutting state threaded through every Build
63	// call. Builder accumulates operators; Tracker is the shared per-pipeline
64	// MemoryTracker (G7a) every memory-bookkeeping operator must use; Config
65	// supplies BatchSize and other runtime knobs.
66	type BuildContext struct {
67		Builder *vectorized.PipelineBuilder
68		Tracker *vectorized.MemoryTracker
69		Config  measure.VectorizedConfig
70	}
71	
72	// PrintTree renders a plan tree as multi-line text. Leaves first column,
73	// each parent indented two spaces deeper than its child. Useful for
74	// debugging analyzer output.
75	func PrintTree(root VecPlan) string {
76		var sb stringBuilder
77		printNode(&sb, root, 0)
78		return sb.String()
79	}
80	
81	func printNode(sb *stringBuilder, node VecPlan, depth int) {
82		for range depth {
83			sb.WriteString("  ")
84		}
85		sb.WriteString(node.String())
86		sb.WriteString("\n")
87		for _, child := range node.Children() {
88			printNode(sb, child, depth+1)
89		}
90	}
91	
92	// stringBuilder is a tiny shim around strings.Builder to keep imports
93	// out of the package-level scope. Inline so test-only helpers don't pull
94	// strings into production builds.
95	type stringBuilder struct{ buf []byte }
96	
97	func (s *stringBuilder) WriteString(str string) { s.buf = append(s.buf, str...) }
98	func (s *stringBuilder) String() string         { return string(s.buf) }

32	// BuildOperators translates the GroupBy + Agg slice of MeasureQueryOptions
33	// into a list of BreakerOperators that, chained after the scan source, form
34	// the vectorized aggregation pipeline.
35	//
36	// Routing rules:
37	//   - GroupBy + Agg both set → emit a single BatchAggregation. The operator's
38	//     own keyIndex map produces per-group buckets and folds the agg slot;
39	//     a separate BatchGroupBy would double the row materialization.
40	//   - Agg set without GroupBy → scalar reduce: a BatchAggregation with no
41	//     key columns. Every row maps to one group, so a single output row is
42	//     emitted carrying the first-seen projected tags plus the agg result,
43	//     matching the row path's aggAllIterator.
44	//   - GroupBy set without Agg → raw GroupBy: a first-seen-row-per-group
45	//     BatchGroupBy. The output preserves the input schema; one row per
46	//     group is emitted in group-insertion order, matching the row path's
47	//     groupIterator + processor.go's current[0] read.
48	//   - Neither set → empty operator list; caller emits raw rows.
49	//
50	// tracker is the per-pipeline MemoryTracker (G7a); it must be non-nil when
51	// any operator is emitted so per-group reservations route to the shared
52	// budget. batchSize controls the operator's output pagination.
53	//
54	// mode selects the BatchAggregation strategy when an agg operator is built
55	// (Agg set): AggModeAll for single-node final reduce; AggModeMap for the
56	// distributed Map phase (G9f.2) that emits typed-column partials. mode is
57	// ignored for the raw-GroupBy branch (BatchGroupBy doesn't carry partial
58	// state — first-seen-row per group is already the final shape).
59	// AggModeReduce is rejected here loudly; its operator is built by the
60	// liaison-side reduce plan (G9f.3), not via BuildOperators.
61	func BuildOperators(
62		opts model.MeasureQueryOptions, schema *vectorized.BatchSchema,
63		tracker *vectorized.MemoryTracker, batchSize int, mode AggMode,
64	) ([]vectorized.BreakerOperator, error) {
65		hasGroupBy := opts.GroupBy != nil && opts.GroupBy.TagFamily != "" && len(opts.GroupBy.TagNames) > 0
66		hasAgg := opts.Agg != nil
67	
68		if !hasGroupBy && !hasAgg {
69			return nil, nil
70		}
71		if tracker == nil {
72			return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: BuildOperators requires a non-nil shared MemoryTracker")
73		}
74		if batchSize <= 0 {
75			return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: batchSize must be > 0, got %d", batchSize)
76		}
77		if mode == AggModeReduce {
78			return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: BuildOperators does not build AggModeReduce — that operator is built by the liaison reduce plan (G9f.3)")
79		}
80	
81		var keyIndices []int
82		if hasGroupBy {
83			var keyErr error
84			keyIndices, keyErr = lookupGroupByKeyIndices(schema, opts.GroupBy)
85			if keyErr != nil {
86				return nil, keyErr
87			}
88		}
89	
90		if !hasAgg {
91			// Raw GroupBy: emit the first-seen row of each group with the
92			// input schema unchanged. entrySize accounts for the per-group
93			// bucket; rowSize is zero because at most one row is retained.
94			pool := vectorized.NewBatchPool(schema, batchSize)
95			gb := NewBatchGroupByFirst(schema, keyIndices, pool, batchSize, tracker, aggEntrySize)
96			return []vectorized.BreakerOperator{gb}, nil
97		}
98	
99		inputIdx, inputErr := lookupAggInputColumnIndex(schema, opts.Agg)
100		if inputErr != nil {
101			return nil, inputErr
102		}
103	
104		aggFn, fnErr := protoAggFuncToInternal(opts.Agg.Func)
105		if fnErr != nil {
106			return nil, fnErr
107		}
108	
109		// The agg result column inherits the target's name — field or tag —
110		// to match the row-path aggregator (aggGroupIterator.Current() in
111		// pkg/query/logical/measure/measure_plan_aggregation.go). Row-path
112		// fixtures expect a single output field named after the original
113		// input (e.g. "value"), not an auto-derived "<field>_<func>" suffix
114		// like "value_sum" — the suffix would break proto.Equal parity in the
115		// integration suite. The aggregation function lives on the operator
116		// spec, not in the column name.
117		//
118		// keyIndices is empty for scalar reduce (Agg without GroupBy):
119		// BatchAggregation.computeKey then returns the same key for every
120		// row, so all rows collapse into a single output row carrying the
121		// first-seen projected tags plus the agg result — the columnar
122		// equivalent of the row path's aggAllIterator.
123		spec := AggSpec{
124			Func:     aggFn,
125			InputCol: inputIdx,
126			Output:   aggTargetName(opts.Agg),
127			HideTag:  opts.Agg.HideTag,
128		}
129		// COUNT_DISTINCT's map-phase precondition (design §7.4 "De-duplicating
130		// the partials", part (a)). computeKey ignores shard id, and a node
131		// holding more than one shard emits one merged partial per group,
132		// labeled with whichever shard's row created it first — a hint, not
133		// an identity. Under replication, staggered shard placement
134		// (pkg/node/round_robin.go's roundRobinSelector) means no two nodes
135		// hold the same shard set, so two nodes' partials for the same group
136		// can collide on that incidental label. Depending on which of the
137		// colliding partials markDedupSeen's (shardID, groupKey) check keeps
138		// vs. drops, the result can either double-count (the survivor still
139		// includes a shard the dropped one also counted) or undercount (the
140		// dropped one carried a shard the survivor never had) — the design
141		// doc's worked 4-node/replicas=1 example walks both outcomes from the
142		// same topology. Forcing one group per (shard, GroupBy-key) makes the
143		// emitted shard_id exact rather than incidental, so only a genuine
144		// replica duplicate can ever share a dedup key.
145		//
146		// This same defect is latent in every distributed agg today, not only
147		// COUNT_DISTINCT — design §7.4 tracks that as a parallel, non-gating
148		// investigation (stage 4a) rather than fixing it here for every
149		// function.
150		if aggFn == AggCountDistinct && mode == AggModeMap {
151			if shardIdx := findShardIDIndex(schema); shardIdx >= 0 {
152				keyIndices = append(keyIndices, shardIdx)
153			}
154		}
155		agg := NewBatchAggregation(schema, keyIndices, []AggSpec{spec},
156			mode, batchSize, tracker, aggEntrySize)
157		return []vectorized.BreakerOperator{agg}, nil
158	}
159	
160	// aggTargetName returns the name the agg result column inherits (design
161	// §5.2): the tag name when Agg targets a tag, otherwise the field name.
162	func aggTargetName(agg *model.MeasureAgg) string {
163		if agg.TagName != "" {
164			return agg.TagName
165		}
166		return agg.FieldName
167	}
168	
169	// BuildTimeBucketOperator builds the BatchTimeBucket operator for a
170	// time-bucketed GroupBy (design §7.2), wrapping upstream directly. Unlike
171	// BuildOperators, this does not return a BreakerOperator to be attached via
172	// PipelineBuilder.Break: BatchTimeBucket is a PullOperator that pulls from
173	// upstream lazily inside its own NextBatch, which is what makes its memory
174	// bound real (see BatchTimeBucket's doc). Callers wire it in via
175	// PipelineBuilder.Transform instead. Check opts.GroupBy.GetTimeBucket() != nil
176	// before calling this rather than BuildOperators.
177	//
178	// tagKeyIndices are the already resolved tag GroupBy keys (empty for a
179	// bucket-only GroupBy, i.e. no tag key at all). Agg is optional, exactly as
180	// for the non-bucketed case: when absent this is a bucketed raw GroupBy
181	// (first-seen row per (bucket, tags)), when present it is a bucketed
182	// aggregate — both shapes reuse the same BatchTimeBucket, since
183	// BatchAggregation with zero AggSpecs already produces the raw-GroupBy
184	// shape. (The analyzer currently rejects the no-Agg case for real requests
185	// — BatchAggregation's empty-AggSpec output layout drops every projected
186	// field, unlike BatchGroupByFirst's full-schema passthrough — but
187	// BuildTimeBucketOperator itself stays agnostic to that policy choice.)
188	func BuildTimeBucketOperator(
189		upstream vectorized.PullOperator, opts model.MeasureQueryOptions, schema *vectorized.BatchSchema,
190		tracker *vectorized.MemoryTracker, batchSize int, mode AggMode,
191	) (*BatchTimeBucket, error) {
192		if tracker == nil {
193			return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: BuildTimeBucketOperator requires a non-nil shared MemoryTracker")
194		}
195		if batchSize <= 0 {
196			return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: batchSize must be > 0, got %d", batchSize)
197		}
198		if mode == AggModeReduce {
199			return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: BuildTimeBucketOperator does not build AggModeReduce — that operator is built by the liaison reduce plan")
200		}
201		var tagKeyIndices []int
202		if opts.GroupBy != nil && opts.GroupBy.TagFamily != "" && len(opts.GroupBy.TagNames) > 0 {
203			var keyErr error
204			tagKeyIndices, keyErr = lookupGroupByKeyIndices(schema, opts.GroupBy)
205			if keyErr != nil {
206				return nil, keyErr
207			}
208		}
209		timestampIdx := schema.TimestampIndex()
210		if timestampIdx < 0 {
211			return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: time_bucket requires a RoleTimestamp column in the scan schema")
212		}
213		var specs []AggSpec
214		var aggFn AggFunc
215		if opts.Agg != nil {
216			inputIdx, inputErr := lookupAggInputColumnIndex(schema, opts.Agg)
217			if inputErr != nil {
218				return nil, inputErr
219			}
220			var fnErr error
221			aggFn, fnErr = protoAggFuncToInternal(opts.Agg.Func)
222			if fnErr != nil {
223				return nil, fnErr
224			}
225			specs = []AggSpec{{
226				Func:     aggFn,
227				InputCol: inputIdx,
228				Output:   aggTargetName(opts.Agg),
229				HideTag:  opts.Agg.HideTag,
230			}}
231		}
232		// Same COUNT_DISTINCT map-phase precondition as BuildOperators (see its
233		// comment for the full derivation): a data node's per-bucket aggregator
234		// can still see rows from more than one of its local shards in a
235		// single upstream batch, so the shard-id column must be part of the
236		// group key — otherwise BatchTimeBucket would merge those shards into
237		// one incidentally-labeled partial per bucket, exactly the shape the
238		// fix in BuildOperators exists to prevent for the unbucketed case.
239		if opts.Agg != nil && aggFn == AggCountDistinct && mode == AggModeMap {
240			if shardIdx := findShardIDIndex(schema); shardIdx >= 0 {
241				tagKeyIndices = append(tagKeyIndices, shardIdx)
242			}
243		}
244		tb := opts.GroupBy.TimeBucket
245		return NewBatchTimeBucket(upstream, schema, tagKeyIndices, timestampIdx, tb.WidthNanos,
246			specs, mode, batchSize, tracker, aggEntrySize, !tb.UseIndexModeMap), nil
247	}
248	
249	// lookupGroupByKeyIndices resolves each GroupBy tag name to its column index
250	// in schema. All names must exist within the configured tag family.
251	func lookupGroupByKeyIndices(schema *vectorized.BatchSchema, gb *model.MeasureGroupBy) ([]int, error) {
252		indices := make([]int, 0, len(gb.TagNames))
253		for _, name := range gb.TagNames {
254			idx := -1
255			for i, def := range schema.Columns {
256				if def.Role == vectorized.RoleTag && def.TagFamily == gb.TagFamily && def.Name == name {
257					idx = i
258					break
259				}
260			}
261			if idx < 0 {
262				return nil, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: GroupBy tag %s.%s not present in schema", gb.TagFamily, name)
263			}
264			indices = append(indices, idx)
265		}
266		return indices, nil
267	}
268	
269	// lookupFieldColumnIndex resolves the agg input field name to its column
270	// index. Only field columns (Role == RoleField) are eligible.
271	func lookupFieldColumnIndex(schema *vectorized.BatchSchema, name string) (int, error) {
272		for i, def := range schema.Columns {
273			if def.Role == vectorized.RoleField && def.Name == name {
274				return i, nil
275			}
276		}
277		return -1, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: Agg field %q not present in schema", name)
278	}
279	
280	// lookupAggInputColumnIndex resolves agg's target column: a tag sibling of
281	// lookupGroupByKeyIndices when agg.TagName is set (matched on RoleTag +
282	// TagFamily + Name, which disambiguates a schema carrying the same tag name in
283	// two families; api/validate.UniqueTagNames rejects that shape on the
284	// registry's create and update paths only, so an older persisted schema can
285	// still carry it), otherwise the existing field lookup.
286	func lookupAggInputColumnIndex(schema *vectorized.BatchSchema, agg *model.MeasureAgg) (int, error) {
287		if agg.TagName == "" {
288			return lookupFieldColumnIndex(schema, agg.FieldName)
289		}
290		for i, def := range schema.Columns {
291			if def.Role == vectorized.RoleTag && def.TagFamily == agg.TagFamily && def.Name == agg.TagName {
292				return i, nil
293			}
294		}
295		return -1, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: Agg tag %s.%s not present in schema", agg.TagFamily, agg.TagName)
296	}

298	// protoAggFuncToInternal maps the proto AggregationFunction enum to the
299	// internal AggFunc constant. UNSPECIFIED is rejected — Aggregation must
300	// name a concrete function.
301	func protoAggFuncToInternal(f modelv1.AggregationFunction) (AggFunc, error) {
302		switch f {
303		case modelv1.AggregationFunction_AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_SUM:
304			return AggSum, nil
305		case modelv1.AggregationFunction_AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_COUNT:
306			return AggCount, nil
307		case modelv1.AggregationFunction_AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_MIN:
308			return AggMin, nil
309		case modelv1.AggregationFunction_AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_MAX:
310			return AggMax, nil
311		case modelv1.AggregationFunction_AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_MEAN:
312			return AggMean, nil
313		case modelv1.AggregationFunction_AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_UNSPECIFIED:
314			return 0, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: Agg.Function is UNSPECIFIED")
315		case modelv1.AggregationFunction_AGGREGATION_FUNCTION_COUNT_DISTINCT:
316			return AggCountDistinct, nil
317		}
318		return 0, fmt.Errorf("vectorized.measure: unknown AggregationFunction %v", f)
319	}
